newsitem.title: USA: Ex-U.S. official criticizes airline, airport safety.
newsitem.headline: Ex-U.S. official criticizes airline, airport safety.

text.p: All nine major U.S. air carriers had good safety records while start-up, discount and commuter airlines had the worst, a former top Transportation Department official said in a CBS "60 Minutes" interview made public on Thursday.

Mary Schiavo, Inspector General from 1990-96, also cited airports named by the Federal Aviation Administration as among the safest -- Honolulu, Houston and San Juan -- and those as the most unsafe -- Chicago, Atlanta and Los Angeles.

Schiavo said nine major airlines, which she did not name, had good safety records, but that among the majors, American, a unit of AMR Corp., Continental Airlines Inc., and Delta Air Lines Inc. had the most accidents.
Schiavo said the carrier with the least accidents was Southwest Airlines Co..

The FAA, part of her department, found the worst records were generally among the start-up, discount and commuter lines, such as AvAtlantic, Mesa Air Group Inc., Rich International, and ValuJet Inc., she said.
Schiavo added that the FAA information, which is not released, should be made readily available to the public.

"The law says government information and government activities are public unless there's a reason to withhold them. And making airlines unhappy is not a legitimate reason," she said in the interview, which will be aired Sunday.
Five weeks ago, the FAA began making available on the Internet its records of airline safety reports and fines.

Schiavo said the unsafe airports were cited because of airport security's inability to find hidden weapons carried by FAA and department employees in a secret audit last year. She told CBS she was identifying them now because the names had been circulated to airline and airport officials.
Schiavo said investigations she made as Inspector General had led to threats that she took seriously enough to move and to keep her address secret for a year.

One of the incidents, she said, was her probe of a training course taken by FAA managers that at one point had people sit around in their underwear with a trainer requiring some to "surrender" their clothing to be sniffed to determine their "essence."
"At taxpayer dollars, we had clothing sniffed," she said.
Schiavo was referring to a 1992 sexual harassment program given FAA employees by an outside contractor, which was ended shortly after the agency learned of it.
In a statement, the FAA said the U.S. aviation system was "the safest in the world." The agency added that $4.4 billion would be spent on safety this year.
